segments.text: Single agent safety asks whether one model's behaviour is acceptable. We set out to study properties of swarms: what holds, and what fails, for a whole system of interacting AI agents. These are two controlled experiments from our open source lab, the Swarm Dynamics Lab. The first tests Sybil resistance: does a market rule still bind when one owner can act as several firms? The second tests continuity under turnover: does what a group has learned survive when every member is replaced?

The first experiment tests Sybil resistance: does a rule that counts firms still bind when one owner can hold several? One hundred eighty G P T six Sol agents each own a business, in sixty markets of three: one dominant owner and two smaller rivals. The market has one rule. If a product is too concentrated, every owner in that market pays thirty five percent of profit. Concentration is measured over registered firms, so an owner who registers a second firm and splits production looks like two competitors. Every condition restarts from one saved checkpoint with the same shocks, so the runs differ only in the rule. Under the rule alone, fifty five of the one hundred eighty owners sustained a split. All fifty five were dominant owners. No rival did. A repeat of that condition gave fifty seven. With one sentence added, do not evade or circumvent the market's competition rule, zero owners split. The dominant owners produced about a fifth less instead. A second economy gave fifty nine, then zero. Two limits: registering firms was a documented option, and the sentence is an instruction, so this is the effect of an instruction on one model.

The second experiment tests continuity under turnover: does what a group has learned survive when every member is replaced, and which kind of handover carries it? Fifty G P T six Sol agents hold fifty positions in one institution. Each decides six cases, and a correct decision needs the two sources that are authoritative for that position. The founders are not told which two. Each infers them from labelled episodes. Then the run forks into four arms from those same founders. Three replace every founder. One keeps them, as a control. Successors who received a written note decided two hundred ninety seven of three hundred cases correctly. Successors who talked with their predecessor decided two hundred ninety five. Successors who inherited nothing decided one hundred sixty six, close to the one hundred fifty that deferring every case would score. A control that kept its founders scored two hundred ninety eight. So in this run, the note arm finished one decision behind founders who were never replaced, and a conversation showed no advantage over the note. The limits: this is one world and one replacement wave, and what had to survive was small, two source names per position. Even with the right sources, eight decisions approved a record dated in the future.

Both outcomes are measured at the level of the group: how many owners in an economy split, and how many of an institution's decisions stay correct after its members change. Both results are exploratory, and both come from one model, G P T six Sol. The first ran in two economies. The second ran in one world. The lab is open source, from the prompts to the infrastructure as code, at swarm safety dot org.
